messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David has been the principal of Northwood High for fifteen years, a role he has always filled with a calm, steady authority. At fifty-two, he was known for his ability to de-escalate any situation, from a food fight in the cafeteria to a tense parent-teacher conference. That sense of professional invulnerability was shattered three months ago in the school’s own parking lot. He had stayed late to meet with the father of a student who had been expelled for violence. As David walked to his car in the fading light, the father cornered him between his sedan and a chain-link fence, his voice low and guttural with rage. Before David could respond, the man shoved him hard against the car door and landed two quick, disorienting punches to his side and head. David remembers raising his arms to shield his face, the cold metal of the car pressing into his back, and the man spitting words he can no longer recall before storming off.

Since that evening, David finds the memory of the assault intrudes unexpectedly. It plays like a short, silent film: the man’s contorted face, the glint of the setting sun on his own car keys clenched in the man’s fist. When these images come to mind, he feels his body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred; his shoulders hunch, and his arms instinctively rise as if to block a blow, a physical echo he can’t control. This physical re-experiencing leaves him with a profound and lingering sense of imminent danger, as if the assault isn't over but merely paused. To his immense frustration, when he tries to deliberately remember what happened, to piece together the sequence of events to make sense of it, he finds it difficult to access the memory. The details feel hazy and slip away, leaving only the raw, intrusive fragments.

In his daily life, David is constantly on edge. He feels jumpy, and a locker slamming down the hall can make him jolt with a surge of adrenaline that leaves him breathless. This hypervigilance has reshaped his relationship with the very building he is meant to command. As soon as he enters any room—the staff lounge, the auditorium for an assembly, even a student’s classroom—his eyes immediately scan for the exits, plotting a mental map of escape before he can even focus on the reason he is there. He has also begun to notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment. In meetings, he finds himself cataloging things on the table: a heavy glass paperweight, a pair of sharp scissors, the metal letter opener on his own desk. They are no longer inert objects but a list of potential threats that he cannot unsee.

This constant, exhausting threat assessment has taken a toll. His wife, Sarah, says it’s like living with a stranger; he startles if she enters a room without announcing herself and can no longer sit with his back to the door in a restaurant. At work, the faculty has noticed his new, brittle demeanor. He feels a chasm opening between the capable leader he was and the frightened man he has become. He finally sought therapy after a fire drill last week. The sudden, piercing sound of the alarm sent him into such a state of panic that he had to lock himself in his office, his heart hammering against his ribs, until it was over. He knew then that he could not go on this way, feeling perpetually unsafe in the one place he had always felt most at home.
